# Reparameterization Estimators

Also called: Reparameterization Trick for Volume Rendering, Reparametrized Gradients

## Overview
Reparameterization Estimators compute gradients of the rendering integral by transforming the integration domain from spatial coordinates to a parameter space (such as opacity or path space) that is independent of the scene parameters $\theta$. This allows the sampling distribution to remain fixed while the integrand absorbs the parameter dependence, enabling stable gradient back-propagation through the sample positions [S1]. Unlike [Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR)](8871-differentiable-direct-volume-rendering.md) which differentiates the discrete summation directly, or [Analytical Gradients](7613-analytical-gradients.md) which derive closed-form derivatives of the continuous integral, this family relies on the reparameterization trick to move the derivative operator inside the expectation [S1].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism relies on the law of the unconscious statistician. Let the rendering integral be $I(\theta) = \int f(x, \theta) dx$. If we can find a transformation $x = g(u, \theta)$ where $u$ is sampled from a distribution $p(u)$ independent of $\theta$, then:
$$
I(\theta) = \int f(g(u, \theta), \theta) p(g(u, \theta)) \left| \frac{\partial g}{\partial u} \right| du = \mathbb{E}_{u \sim p(u)} [ \hat{f}(u, \theta) ]
$$
The gradient is then:
$$
\nabla_\theta I(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{u \sim p(u)} [ \nabla_\theta \hat{f}(u, \theta) ]
$$
In volume rendering, the most common reparameterization is via the cumulative opacity (CDF) $F_r(t) = 1 - \exp(-\int_{t_n}^t \sigma(s) ds)$. By sampling $u \sim U[0,1]$ and setting $t = F_r^{-1}(u)$, the randomness is decoupled from $\sigma$. The gradient flows through the inverse CDF evaluation and the radiance evaluation at $t$ [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md)
A technique that computes color estimates by sampling points on a ray using the inverse of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the density field. It solves the problem of computing gradients with respect to the density field parameters by making the sampling locations differentiable functions of the density, allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sample positions. Unlike [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)'s hierarchical sampling which uses an auxiliary coarse model trained separately, this method learns sampling points end-to-end without auxiliary networks. Compared to standard [importance sampling](#9521-importance-sampling.md) with uniform distribution, this stratified reparameterized sampling exhibits lower variance.

### [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md)
The [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](#3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md) is a method for estimating the derivatives of the path integral in [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) with respect to object shape parameters. It solves the problem of computing gradients when scene geometry depends on parameters $\theta$, by separating the differentiation of the path integral into interior and boundary terms. Unlike its siblings [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md) and [Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering](4798-reparameterized-monte-carlo-volume-rendering.md), which typically rely on differentiable sampling within the volume or standard CDF inversion, this method converts interior volume integrals into boundary area integrals using the divergence theorem. This eliminates the need to evaluate the deformation mapping inside the volume, avoiding expensive tetrahedralizations.

### [Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering](4798-reparameterized-monte-carlo-volume-rendering.md)
[Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering](#4798-reparameterized-monte-carlo-volume-rendering.md) is a differentiable volume rendering method that estimates expected radiance by sampling from the density-induced probability distribution using the reparameterization trick. It allows end-to-end gradient-based optimization of [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) without auxiliary models, alleviating the computational costs associated with the color component by requiring only a few radiance field evaluations per ray. It sets itself apart from [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md) by explicitly defining the sampling distribution via the opacity CDF and solving for ray distances via inverse opacity, and from [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md) by focusing on discrete ray sampling rather than boundary path integrals.

### [Reparametrized Integral Gradients](6785-reparametrized-integral-gradients.md)
A method that reparametrizes relevant integrals (including pixel integrals over spherical domains) to remove dependency on scene parameters, thereby eliminating discontinuities during parameter changes.

### Bidirectional Estimator for Implicit Surfaces
#### definition
- [S1] A Monte Carlo estimator for differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces that performs better than [unidirectional estimators](#3538-unidirectional-volume-boundary-estimator.md) in scenes with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials.
#### pitfall
- [S1] Unidirectional estimators struggle with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials, leading to noisier gradients and less accurate reconstructions.
#### comparison
- [S1] Performs better than unidirectional estimators in scenes with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials, producing cleaner derivative images and smoother optimized shapes.

## Background
The reparameterization trick was originally introduced by [Kingma and Welling (2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114) for variational autoencoders. In the context of differentiable rendering, it was adapted to handle the non-differentiable nature of sampling from distributions dependent on learnable parameters. The specific application to volume rendering via opacity CDF inversion was detailed in [Mildenhall et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934) (NeRF) and further refined in subsequent works on differentiable path tracing and [implicit surface rendering](#775-differentiable-volumetric-rendering-dvr.md) [S1]. The Boundary Path Integral Formulation was introduced by [Zhang et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3641519.3657473) to handle shape derivatives without tetrahedralization [S2].
